title: How to Block Ads on OpenWrt | Network-Wide Ad Blocking
description:
With OpenWrt, you can block advertising and tracking domains across your network using the Adblock package, without installing a separate Pi-hole server or configuring ad blockers on individual devices.

In this video, I demonstrate how to install and configure Adblock on an OpenWrt router and test DNS-based ad blocking in a real network environment.

I start by explaining how DNS-based ad blocking works and how it prevents devices from resolving domains associated with advertisements and tracking.

Then I explore the available Adblock packages, install Adblock and its LuCI interface, and configure the DNS backend and blocklist sources.

I also configure Force Local DNS to redirect standard DNS requests through the router, helping prevent clients from bypassing the local DNS filtering through external DNS servers.

Finally, I test domain blocking, examine DNS responses, and configure DNS reporting to monitor DNS queries and blocked domains.

⏱️ Video Chapters:

To be added based on the final video timestamps.

🔑 Key Takeaways:

- Network-Wide Ad Blocking: OpenWrt can filter advertising and tracking domains for devices using the router's DNS service.
- Adblock Package: The Adblock package provides DNS-based domain filtering directly on OpenWrt.
- LuCI Interface: luci-app-adblock provides a web interface for managing Adblock settings, blocklists, and reports.
- DNS Blocklists: Multiple blocklist sources can be used to identify and block advertising and tracking domains.
- Force Local DNS: Redirects standard DNS requests on port 53 to the router's local DNS service.
- **DNS Reporting:** Uses tcpdump to capture DNS traffic and generate reports about DNS requests and blocked domains.
- Testing: DNS lookups can be used to verify whether selected domains are being blocked.
- Limitations: DNS-based filtering cannot reliably block advertisements served from the same domains as legitimate content, including most YouTube ads.

⚠️ Important Note:

DNS-based ad blocking does not guarantee that every advertisement will be blocked. Its effectiveness depends on the selected blocklists, DNS configuration, and how applications deliver advertisements.

Force Local DNS redirects conventional DNS traffic on port 53, but it does not automatically prevent clients from using encrypted DNS protocols such as DNS over HTTPS (DoH).

DNS reporting requires a properly configured Report Interface and a working tcpdump installation. After enabling reporting or changing the Report Interface, restart the Adblock service to initialize DNS capture.

title: WinBox 3 No Longer Works with MikroTik RouterOS 7.25!
description:
With the release of MikroTik RouterOS 7.25, WinBox 3 can no longer connect to routers running this version. MikroTik now requires WinBox 4.3 or newer.

In this video, I explain what changed in RouterOS 7.25, why WinBox 3 is no longer compatible, and what MikroTik administrators need to know before upgrading their routers.

I start by examining the new minimum WinBox version requirement and explaining why older versions, including WinBox 3.43, can no longer connect to RouterOS 7.25.

Then I demonstrate the connection issue, download and set up WinBox 4, and connect to a MikroTik router running RouterOS 7.25.

I also take a look at the differences between WinBox 3 and WinBox 4, including interface changes, compatibility, and considerations when migrating saved router connections.

Finally, I discuss what this change means for network administrators and why it's important to check management tool compatibility before upgrading RouterOS, especially on remote or production routers.

⏱️ Video Chapters:

00:00 - Introduction: WinBox 3 and RouterOS 7.25
00:45 - Why WinBox 3 No Longer Connects
02:10 - Downloading and Setting Up WinBox 4
04:15 - Connecting to RouterOS 7.25 with WinBox 4
05:50 - WinBox 4 Interface Changes and Migration Tips
07:20 - Summary and Final Thoughts

🔑 Key Takeaways:

- RouterOS 7.25: MikroTik introduced a minimum supported WinBox version of 4.3.
- WinBox 3 Compatibility: WinBox 3.43 and earlier versions can no longer connect to RouterOS 7.25.
- Connection Error: Older WinBox versions display the "router requires newer winbox" error.
- WinBox 4: Use WinBox 4.3 or newer to manage routers running RouterOS 7.25.
- Interface Changes: WinBox 4 introduces a redesigned interface and native support for Windows, Linux, and macOS.
- Saved Connections: Legacy CDB files can be imported into WinBox 4, while older WBX files are not directly supported.
- RouterOS Upgrades: Check WinBox compatibility and keep an alternative management method available before upgrading production routers.

⚠️ Important Note:

WinBox 3 has not stopped working with every MikroTik router. The compatibility restriction applies to RouterOS 7.25 and versions enforcing the new minimum WinBox requirement.

A CDB file contains saved WinBox connection information and is not a RouterOS configuration backup.

Before upgrading RouterOS on a production router, back up your configuration and make sure you have a compatible version of WinBox or an alternative management method, such as SSH.

title: I Let Claude Configure My MikroTik Router. Here’s What Happened
description:
In this video, I test whether Claude AI can actually configure a MikroTik router.

Instead of manually configuring RouterOS myself, I give Claude SSH access to a MikroTik router and let it build a complete network configuration based on a real-world scenario.

I use Claude in VS Code as the AI agent. Claude connects to the MikroTik through SSH, inspects the existing configuration, identifies the RouterOS version and hardware, and then configures the router step by step.

The goal is not simply to generate MikroTik commands. Claude has to inspect, configure, troubleshoot, and validate a real network device.

The target configuration includes:

- A main LAN with normal Internet access
- A separate VPN network using an L2TP VPN connection
- A guest network with MikroTik HotSpot authentication

The VPN network uses policy-based routing so its traffic goes through the L2TP VPN, while the main network continues using the normal WAN connection.

The guest network is isolated from the internal networks and uses MikroTik HotSpot for authentication.

Claude also configures DHCP, DNS, NAT, routing, policy routing, firewall rules, bridges, wireless networks, and network isolation.

One interesting part of the experiment is the management connection. The initial Wi-Fi and management path changes during the configuration, so Claude has to handle the network change, reconnect to the router, and continue the configuration.

After the configuration is complete, I test the actual network behavior, including Internet access, VPN routing, HotSpot authentication, firewall isolation, and SSH management.

Finally, I review what Claude configured, what required troubleshooting, and what still needs to be manually verified.

This is not a traditional MikroTik configuration tutorial. It is a practical experiment to see how far an AI agent can actually go when it has SSH access to a real network device.

title: MikroTik Reverse Proxy: Host Multiple Websites on One Public IP
description:
In this MikroTik Reverse Proxy tutorial, I show you how to host multiple web applications with different domains on a single public IP address and secure them with HTTPS.

Using MikroTik RouterOS built-in Reverse Proxy, we'll route incoming requests to the correct internal application based on the requested domain name. This gives us a clean way to publish multiple web services to the internet without needing a separate public IP address for each application.

For this demonstration, I'm using a MikroTik CHR with three containerized web applications: Homepage, File Browser, and IT-Tools. Each application runs on its own internal IP address and port, while MikroTik handles the public HTTPS connections and routes the traffic to the correct backend.

You'll also learn how SNI (Server Name Indication) allows MikroTik to identify which domain the client is requesting and send the connection to the correct backend application, even though all three domains use the same public IP address.
